stories.headline: BHV Marais Aims to Reopen for Crucial Holiday Season Amid Safety Upgrades
stories.claim: Paris department store BHV Marais, shut since 9 November, aims to reopen for Christmas after insurance issue settled and safety works begin.
stories.summary: Paris department store BHV Marais, which abruptly locked its doors on 9 November, says it hopes to reopen in time for the Christmas season. CEO Karl-Stéphane Cottendin said in a statement that the insurance problem cited for the closure has been resolved and the store is now fully insured to operate. Negotiations with the landlord and court-appointed administrator Brookfield have paved the way for fire-safety upgrades, which will extend the closure, and no reopening date has been set. The store filed for court protection on 28 October, blaming cash-flow problems on Brookfield. Brands left in large numbers after the controversial Shein partnership under the previous owner, and the group's second store outside Paris is still under separate review. Staff across both sites will stay on full pay during the closure.

No reopening date has been given; the aim is to be open for Christmas and January.

All employees across both stores will continue to be paid during the closure.

stories.headline: TG Jones put up for sale by private equity firm after less than 18 months
stories.claim: Private equity owner Modella Capital has put TG Jones, the former WH Smith high street business, up for sale less than 18 months after buying it.
stories.summary: Modella Capital is putting TG Jones, the rebranded former WH Smith high street chain, up for sale less than 18 months after buying it for around £42 million in 2025. The private equity firm has closed more than 100 stores in a court-approved restructuring, leaving 346 sites, and expects dozens more closures, which would bring the total to around 150. The business employs about 3,500 people. Modella has hired Teneo to run the sale after receiving unsolicited approaches, and a deal is not expected before the first quarter of 2027. The move comes as discount chain Poundland, which Modella had looked at, is seeking new owners and has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators.

Shoppers will be able to scan an NFC chip or QR code to see product composition, material origins and environmental impact. Another Tomorrow will be the first brand to use the combined service, with a rollout planned before the end of 2026. The deal comes as the EU prepares its Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, with textile requirements expected to be unveiled in 2027. Aura, now more than 50 brands strong, is led by new chief executive Marcel Härtlein as it shifts from a blockchain platform toward an industry service provider.

stories.headline: Mongolia’s president to resign over railway corruption allegations
stories.claim: Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa announced he will resign over allegations he took $25 million in bribes linked to a railway contract.
stories.summary: Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa has announced he will resign after the opposition Democratic Party accused him of taking $25 million in bribes linked to a government railway project. The allegation, made by former Ulaanbaatar mayor Nyambaatar Khishgee, concerns a 2019 contract for the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway, which carries coal to China, awarded to Bodi International without competitive tender. Bodi denies paying cash bribes. Khurelsukh insists he is being falsely accused but says he will step down to restore his name. Parliament, the 126-seat State Great Khural, must approve the resignation and is expected to vote this week; the speaker would then act as interim president. Two other officials named in the allegations also said they would resign. The political turmoil follows three prime ministers in nine months.
key_points: Khurelsukh, president since 2021, said on Tuesday he will resign and that he is being falsely accused.

If accepted, the parliament speaker becomes interim president.

stories.market_take: Mongolia's coal export route to China is a sensitive asset, but the political change is unlikely to move global markets much.

stories.headline: New York Fashion Week Fight: 2294 and Signet Sue N4XT in Catwalk Case
stories.claim: Signet Fashion and 2294 sue N4XT in Manhattan federal court over ownership of the New York Fashion Week brand.
stories.summary: A legal fight over who owns New York Fashion Week has moved into Manhattan federal court, with Signet Fashion and the trademark holder 2294 suing N4XT in a 59-page complaint. The suit says N4XT wrongly presents itself as the owner and operator of NYFW, despite 2294 having bought the federal and international trademarks, the nyfw.com domain and official social accounts, with about 9.19 million followers, last June. The dispute grows out of a joint venture, KFN Events, in which KF Fashion holds 51 percent and N4XT is the minority partner. The plaintiffs claim N4XT took a $5 million investment meant to run events and used it to build its own brand, and then walked away. N4XT's co-founder Abell denies the claims and plans a counter-suit for tortious interference. Trademark expert Susan Scafidi notes that no one has clearly owned the name, which makes the case a wider test of control over the industry's signature event.

stories.headline: The Great Fashion Reset
stories.claim: Fashion's creative director reshuffle is expected to slow in 2026 as recent appointments settle, though further moves remain possible.
stories.summary: Fashion's great creative director reshuffle may be levelling off, according to executive search specialists quoted by WWD, after a year in which Dior, Chanel, Gucci, Balenciaga, Celine, Loewe, Givenchy and several others changed designers. Jonathan Anderson moved from Loewe to Dior after 11 years, while Olivier Rousteing stepped down from Balenciaga after 14 years and Véronique Nichanian ended 37 years at Hermès, with Grace Wales Bonner set to succeed her. Consultants say most recent appointments should succeed, but warn that some brands still have open creative chairs or may rethink their choices. Prada's separation from Versace's new creative director Dario Vitale, shortly after Prada completed its acquisition, has left the house looking for a successor. Sources name Pieter Mulier of Alaïa as the lead candidate, though that remains unconfirmed.

stories.headline: Global Luxury Market Poised for Long-Term Growth
stories.claim: Bain and Altagamma forecast the global luxury market to reach 2.2 to 2.6 trillion euros by 2035, with personal luxury flat-to-slightly up in 2026.
stories.summary: The global luxury market is forecast to grow from 1.52 trillion euros in 2026 to between 2.2 and 2.6 trillion euros by 2035, a 4 to 6 percent annual rate, according to the fall 2026 Bain-Altagamma Luxury Worldwide Market Monitor. The report presented in Milan sees longevity as a growing driver, as older consumers account for roughly 45 to 55 percent of luxury spending. Personal luxury goods are expected to recover modestly, reaching 367 billion euros in 2026 with 1 to 3 percent growth at current rates, while experiential luxury such as hospitality, yachts and cruises grows faster. Regionally, the Americas are expected to lead personal luxury growth, while mainland China is forecast to decline 1 to 3 percent and the Middle East, Africa and Oceania to contract sharply. The authors also warn that AI is changing how consumers find brands, giving companies less control over their image.
key_points: The luxury market is forecast to reach 2.2 to 2.6 trillion euros by 2035, up from 1.52 trillion euros in 2026.
Personal luxury goods are expected to reach 367 billion euros in 2026, with modest growth.
Longevity is seen as a key growth driver, with older generations holding about half of luxury spending.
The Americas are forecast to grow 7 to 9 percent at constant currency, while mainland China falls 1 to 3 percent.
Experiential luxury, including hospitality and cruises, is growing faster than traditional goods.
The report says AI search is reducing brands' control over how they are discovered.
stories.market_take: Modest forecast growth for personal luxury goods suggests a steady rather than strong outlook for listed luxury groups.

stories.claim: Target's third-quarter sales rose 7.1% and profits beat forecasts, prompting a raised annual outlook, though apparel sales fell.
stories.summary: Target posted its best quarterly sales growth since 2022, with third-quarter sales up 7.1%, and earnings per share of $2.65 far ahead of the $2.08 analysts expected. Net profit rose 76% to $1.2 billion on net sales of $27.1 billion. The US retailer raised its full-year sales growth forecast to about 6% and its EPS guidance to $10.65 to $11.40. Apparel and accessories sales fell 3.8% to $3.7 billion, a drag that management says it is working to fix, with chief executive Michael Fiddelke and the returning creative director Isaac Mizrahi leading the push. Shares rose 4% to $165.93 after the results. Analysts at UBS and GlobalData were positive about the quarter's momentum into the holiday season.
key_points: Third-quarter sales rose 7.1%, the strongest quarter since 2022, with comparable sales up 4.6% in stores and 9.8% online.
Earnings per share were $2.65 against analyst expectations of $2.08, helped by a $301 million benefit from tariff refunds.
Full-year sales growth guidance was raised to about 6% and EPS guidance to $10.65 to $11.40.
Apparel and accessories sales fell 3.8% to $3.7 billion, with women's apparel and shoes the main problem areas.
Capital spending is set to reach about $5 billion this year and $5 billion to $6 billion next year.
Shares rose 4% to $165.93 on Wednesday.
stories.market_take: Strong beat and raised guidance should support sentiment towards US discount and general retailers into the holiday season.

stories.headline: Report: Microplastic Leaks from Synthetic Clothing Waste Nearly Quadruple
stories.claim: A report commissioned by Cotton Incorporated estimates synthetic clothing waste leaked 878,000 tonnes of microplastics in 2024.
stories.summary: Discarded synthetic clothing released an estimated 878,000 metric tons of microplastics into the environment in 2024, almost four times the modelled figure for 2000, according to a new report. The estimate ranges from 588,000 to 1.11 million tons. The report, titled The Microplastic Ticking Time Bomb, was produced by the Swiss research consultancy Earth Action, but Cotton Incorporated commissioned and funded it, and its chief sustainability officer co-authored it. Garments dumped in the open make up about 5% of synthetic clothing deposited but 90% of 2024 leakage. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for 45% of leakage, and the authors say peer review is still pending.
key_points: Synthetic clothing waste released an estimated 878,000 metric tons of microplastics in 2024, with a range of 588,000 to 1.11 million tons.
That is nearly four times the modelled 2000 total, driven by decades of accumulated waste.
Cotton Incorporated commissioned and funded the report, and its chief sustainability officer co-authored it, which Earth Action says did not affect the conclusions.
Open-dumped garments are about 5% of deposited synthetic clothing but 90% of 2024 leakage.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for about 45% of 2024 leakage, with East and Southeast Asia at 18% and South Asia at 15%.
Independent peer review through the Plastic Footprint Network is still pending, with results expected around the end of 2026.

stories.headline: TJX Lifts Annual Forecast on Strong Holiday Demand, Shares Jump
stories.claim: TJX raised its full-year outlook after beating third-quarter sales estimates, and its shares jumped about 10%.
stories.summary: TJX, owner of TJ Maxx, Marshalls and HomeGoods, lifted its full-year outlook on Wednesday, and its shares rose about 10% in early trading, putting them on course for their best day in six years. Third-quarter revenue was $15.95 billion against analyst estimates of $15.84 billion. The company now expects comparable sales growth of 4% in fiscal 2027, up from 3% to 4%, and adjusted EPS of $5.17 to $5.20. US shoppers are trading down to off-price chains as sticky inflation and higher fuel prices bite. Rival Ross Stores rose 3% ahead of its own results on Thursday.

Adjusted EPS guidance was narrowed and nudged up to $5.17 to $5.20.
Third-quarter revenue of $15.95 billion beat analysts' average estimate of $15.84 billion.
Marmaxx, the apparel-focused division, grew comparable sales just 2%, lagging other divisions.
Fuel and freight costs are the main headwind into the fourth quarter.
Ross Stores is due to report on Thursday, with its shares already up 3%.

stories.headline: Plastic Shoes Are in Their Luxury Era
stories.claim: Plastic shoes are moving into high fashion, with luxury houses such as Saint Laurent, LOEWE and Yeezy showing transparent and PVC footwear.
stories.summary: Plastic footwear, long a cheap novelty, has become a luxury fashion trend, with Saint Laurent, LOEWE and Yeezy all showing transparent and PVC designs. Saint Laurent's Fall/Winter 2026 pointed TPU slingbacks and its Spring/Summer 2027 menswear clear polyurethane derbies are examples, the latter worn by actor Alexander Skarsgård on the red carpet. Melissa, the Brazilian jelly-shoe brand, has repositioned itself through collaborations with Y/Project, Undercover and Diesel. The writer traces the lineage from 1990s jelly sandals and Prada's acrylic sandals to Balenciaga Crocs and Bottega Veneta's rubber boots. Some of these pieces now sell for around $1,000.

stories.headline: Kering Hires Group Pricing Director: Why It Matters
stories.claim: Kering has created a group pricing director role and appointed Francisco Ochando, a former Nike and Inditex executive, to it.
stories.summary: Kering has created a new group-level role of pricing director and given it to Francisco Ochando, who started on 16 November and reports to chief product officer Marilyne Trebus. The appointment is part of CEO Luca de Meo's ReconKering strategy, which seeks to centralise some functions while keeping brand identities distinct. The luxury group is grappling with pricing criticism after the post-Covid boom, and Gucci has cut some prices, such as the Mercato tote, which fell 20% to 25%. Analysts say the move fits a need for greater discipline after years of underperformance, though some question why pricing needs group oversight.
key_points: Francisco Ochando joined Kering as group pricing director on 16 November and reports to chief product officer Marilyne Trebus.
He previously worked at Inditex, Calvin Klein and Nike, most recently as director of planning for lifestyle footwear at Nike.

stories.headline: France's Engie chief rejects nationalisation call by presidential hopeful Melenchon
stories.claim: Engie's CEO rejected a call by French presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon to renationalise the energy group.
stories.summary: Engie chief executive Catherine MacGregor has rejected a plan by hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon to renationalise the energy group. Speaking after a dinner on Tuesday that brought together Mélenchon and French business leaders, including TotalEnergies' Patrick Pouyanné and LVMH's Bernard Arnault, MacGregor said Engie could invest in France without state ownership. The French state holds 23% of Engie. Mélenchon is tipped to lead the left in the spring presidential election, and polls suggest he could reach a run-off against Marine Le Pen. His platform includes restoring retirement at 60, phasing out nuclear power and capping some prices.
key_points: Engie CEO Catherine MacGregor said renationalisation was unnecessary for investment in France and renewables.
The French state holds a 23% stake in Engie after once owning it outright.
Mélenchon attended a dinner on Tuesday with business leaders including TotalEnergies' Patrick Pouyanné, LVMH's Bernard Arnault and Renault's Jean-Dominique Senard.
Mélenchon's platform includes repealing the pension overhaul, raising the minimum wage, capping some prices and phasing out nuclear power.
Polls suggest Mélenchon could reach a run-off, where he would likely lose to Marine Le Pen.
MacGregor also criticised Le Pen's energy plans, including leaving the European electricity market.
stories.market_take: A stronger chance of a leftist government could weigh on French utilities such as Engie and on French equities more broadly.

stories.headline: 40 Years On, the Musée des Arts Décoratifs’ Fashion Collection Remains Ahead of Its Time
stories.claim: Paris's Musée des Arts Décoratifs marks 40 years of its fashion collection with a new exhibition running to April 2027.
stories.summary: Paris's Musée des Arts Décoratifs is celebrating four decades of its self-contained fashion collection with an exhibition called "Look: 40 Years of Fashion at the Museum", open until 4 April 2027. The central Nef hall showcases one look from 40 of the museum's more than 70 past shows, while surrounding galleries reveal the work of atelier craftspeople and museum conservators. Curator Sophie Lemahieu told Harper's Bazaar that the museum has helped win fashion recognition as a serious art-history field, a battle that was far from settled when the collection was formalised in 1986. The show also highlights how fashion became a matter of national prestige in France, notably after the Louvre's Cour Carrée began hosting ready-to-wear shows in 1982. The exhibition is a useful reminder of how the institution shaped the way fashion is curated worldwide.
key_points: The Musée de la Mode et du Textile, the fashion arm of the Musée des Arts Décoratifs, turns 40 this year.
The exhibition "Look: 40 Years of Fashion at the Museum" runs until 4 April 2027.

Curators say fashion has moved from being dismissed in museums to being a standard exhibition subject.

stories.headline: VF Could Sell Vans, But it Probably Won’t
stories.claim: VF's CFO says the company could sell Vans but is likely to keep it, as the brand has shrunk to about $2 billion in sales.
stories.summary: VF Corp's chief financial officer, Abhishek Dalmia, said the company could sell Vans but probably will not, preferring to keep the option of stabilising the brand. Speaking at J.P. Morgan's Global Brands and Luxury Conference in Paris, he said Vans was once a $4 billion business built on just five product silhouettes, and has since fallen to about $2 billion. Dalmia argued that Vans need not grow for VF to become a strong company again, and that its fixed-cost base could deliver significant profit once sales stabilise. Chief executive Bracken Darrell said Vans order books were improving and expects the brand to show improvement in the second half. He also pointed to growth at Timberland, The North Face and Altra, which he said has risen from $60 million at acquisition to over $300 million. The comments matter for investors weighing VF's turnaround under its current management.
key_points: VF's CFO Abhishek Dalmia said the group could sell Vans but prefers to keep it for now.
Vans has fallen from about $4 billion in sales to roughly $2 billion, built on five product silhouettes.
Management expects Vans to show improvement in the second half, after weak second-quarter results last month.
CEO Bracken Darrell said Altra has grown from $60 million to more than $300 million since acquisition.
VF plans to expand Timberland's own-store distribution in the US and then Europe.
stories.market_take: Investors may see Vans as a drag that management is unlikely to sell soon, so VF's turnaround depends on its outdoor brands.

stories.headline: How Celine’s Michael Rider Quietly Seized Fashion’s Attention
stories.claim: Michael Rider's Celine has won over fashion and menswear fans in under two years, with a clear, accessible vision.
stories.summary: Michael Rider, artistic director of Celine since 2025, has rapidly won over fashion's critics and buyers with a clearer, more wearable vision for the LVMH-owned house. His latest Paris menswear-leaning co-ed show, staged in October, drew celebrity guests and was built on tailoring for men, floppy blazers and cropped cigarette trousers. Rider has also delivered a hit sneaker, a Reebok collaboration reissuing the 1982 Freestyle Lo in leather, which sold out. He previously worked at Balenciaga and under Phoebe Philo at Celine, and then as creative director of women's Polo Ralph Lauren, where he learned to make collections legible. He succeeded Hedi Slimane, whose skinny rock-era look he has replaced. The profile suggests Rider has reset Celine's direction, which matters for LVMH's fashion business.

stories.headline: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
stories.claim: UN report finds one in four women worldwide cannot refuse sex within marriage, with the rate highest in West and Central Africa.
stories.summary: One in four women around the world have no real power to refuse sex with their husband or partner, according to a new UN Population Fund report published on Thursday. The figure rises to 45% in west and central Africa and 33% in east and southern Africa and Arab states, while about one in ten women in Latin America and the Caribbean face the same constraint. Girls aged 15 to 19 have even less ability to say no than women aged 45 to 49, based on analysis of eight countries with comparable data. Campaigners say marital rape is still not criminalised in several African countries, with seven expressly exempting husbands from prosecution. The report puts pressure on governments to align marriage and rape laws with the Maputo Protocol.
key_points: UNFPA report says one in four women globally cannot refuse sex with their husband or partner.

stories.headline: North Korea’s Kim visits university as speculation mounts over Trump talks
stories.claim: Kim Jong Un made public appearances at a naval university as speculation grows over a possible Trump meeting in China during APEC.
stories.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has been seen in state media visiting a naval university and construction sites, fuelling speculation that he could meet US President Donald Trump during the APEC summit in China. Trump arrived in Shenzhen on 18 November for talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, and said in Manila that Kim 'would like to' meet. Beijing said it had 'no information' on any meeting, and Pyongyang has not responded. Analysts point to Kim's recent visit to Mount Paektu, a sacred site he often visits before major decisions, as a possible sign of a trip to Shenzhen, and say Beijing could provide a jet as it did for the 2018 Singapore summit. Previous Trump-Kim summits produced no concrete deal, and North Korea has enshrined its nuclear status in law.
key_points: Kim visited a naval university on the east coast on 18 November and urged training of naval combat experts.

stories.headline: Europe argued over who would talk to Russia. Agreeing what to say is even tougher.
stories.claim: EU countries debate whether to demand maximal concessions from Russia or pursue confidence-building steps in future Ukraine talks.
stories.summary: European governments are split over how to approach any negotiations with Russia on Ukraine, with the question of what to say now proving harder than deciding who speaks. EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas wants Europe to open with maximal demands on Russia, while Austria proposes a 15-point paper with limited ceasefires and an international monitoring forum. Norway's foreign minister urged the use of Cold War-era principles such as the 1975 Helsinki Accords. Baltic and eastern flank states back Kallas's sequencing, insisting on a ceasefire before peace talks. The European team comprises France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the UK, NATO and EU representatives, and EU officials expect talks to resume in Abu Dhabi within weeks despite daily Russian attacks on Ukraine.
key_points: Kallas wants Europe to demand maximum concessions from Russia up front, then set out its red lines.
Austria's 15-point paper proposes partial ceasefires and an international forum to monitor any peace deal.

stories.headline: England and Wales to scrap leasehold system, cap ground rent at £250
stories.claim: England and Wales would ban most new leasehold flats and cap ground rent at £250 a year under a proposed Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill.
stories.summary: The UK government is introducing a Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill that would eventually ban the sale of virtually all new leasehold homes in England and Wales, with the bill due in Parliament on Thursday 19 November 2026. Housing minister Matthew Pennycook called the current system an 'anachronism' that is 'blighting lives'. The first measure is a £250 annual cap on ground rent, expected in 2028 through secondary legislation, falling to a peppercorn after 40 years. The bill would also abolish forfeiture, so homeowners cannot lose their homes over relatively small unpaid debts, make it easier to switch to commonhold with the agreement of half a block's residents, and improve service charge transparency. The new-build leasehold ban is expected to come into force after the next election. Further measures, including a property management regulator, will follow in a second law. Freeholders say the policy is unjust and could wipe £18.7bn from investments overnight, while campaigners warn that existing leaseholders could be left behind.
key_points: The bill would eventually ban the sale of most new leasehold homes in England and Wales.
Ground rent would be capped at £250 a year from 2028, falling to a peppercorn after 40 years.
Forfeiture would be abolished, ending evictions over relatively small unpaid bills.
Switching to commonhold would need only half of a block's residents to agree.
Freeholders say the policy could wipe £18.7bn from investments overnight.
Campaigners warn existing leaseholders could be left behind, as converting existing buildings remains unresolved.
stories.market_take: Freehold investors and listed property-related firms could face pressure if the reforms proceed; no specific listed stocks are clearly affected.

stories.headline: Colombia Rejects Joint Plan With U.S. to Target Drug Gangs
stories.claim: Colombia's president reportedly rejected a US plan for joint military operations on its soil, while Colombia joined a US anti-cartel coalition.
stories.summary: Colombia has turned down a Trump administration plan for joint US military operations against drug gangs on its soil, according to the New York Times, which says President Abelardo De La Espriella lacked the legislative votes to approve US troops operating in the country. The reporting sits awkwardly beside a separate US account that Colombia had authorised joint operations and joined the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking at an anti-cartel conference in Panama, said Bogota had requested Pentagon participation and signed a memorandum with Colombian Defence Minister Jorge Mora. The dispute matters because it tests how far Washington can extend its boat-strike campaign, which has reportedly killed at least 215 people, into land operations in Latin America.
key_points: The New York Times reported that President De La Espriella told US officials he would not agree to joint military operations on Colombian soil because he lacked legislative support.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said in Panama that Colombia had authorised joint operations against narco-terrorist networks and was officially joining the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition.
Colombia follows Peru in joining the Shield of the Americas, an anti-cartel alliance led by Trump that includes Argentina, Ecuador and El Salvador.
Hegseth visited Bogotá on Wednesday, and Gen. Dan Caine recently met Colombian military leaders, showing that cooperation continues despite the dispute.
Legal experts and rights groups say US strikes on alleged drug boats could amount to extrajudicial killings, and the reported push for land strikes raises the same questions.
The accounts of Colombia's position conflict, so the true state of the agreement remains unclear.

stories.headline: 7 people, company charged over false work pass declarations; some workers deployed at Changi Airport
stories.claim: Seven people and a cleaning firm were charged in Singapore over false work pass declarations, with some workers placed at Changi Airport.
stories.summary: Seven individuals and a cleaning and facilities company were charged in Singapore on Thursday over false declarations in work pass applications, with some foreign workers allegedly deployed at Changi Airport. Double Huat director Ng Leong Huat faces four charges over false Employment Pass declarations and one for misleading a Ministry of Manpower inspector. Re Sustainability Cleantech faces charges for inflating salaries in 20 work pass applications by adding overtime, with 19 of those workers allegedly sent to clean at Changi. Six others face charges linked to abuse of Training Employment Pass applications, where workers were allegedly recruited for cleaning and food work instead of training. The case highlights enforcement against work pass abuse, with penalties of up to S$20,000 and two years' jail per offence.

Ng Leong Huat allegedly made false declarations about four Employment Pass holders and misled a MOM inspector.

stories.headline: 5 key places that signal where Spain’s election is heading
stories.claim: Spain's 29 November snap election is set to see the conservative PP lead, with Vox in third and Sánchez's Socialists trailing.
stories.summary: Spain's snap general election on 29 November looks set to reshape the country's electoral map, with polls pointing to a historic defeat for Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialists. The centre-right People's Party leads the polls, while the far-right Vox is projected to take third place with about 18% of the vote, enough to help the conservatives form a coalition. Politico Europe highlights five regions to watch, including Seville, which the Socialists have won in every election since 1977 but could lose to the PP. Other key tests include Aragón's bellwether status, the Basque Country where left-wing nationalist EH Bildu may win its first region-wide victory, Catalonia's kingmaker role and Murcia, where the PP and Vox could take most seats. Fragmentation on the left further reduces Sánchez's chances of forming a government.
key_points: Spain holds a snap general election on 29 November, with polls showing the People's Party in the lead.
The Socialists are trailing in second place, and Seville could be lost for the first time since 1977.
Vox is projected to take third place with around 18% of the vote, potentially giving the right a coalition majority.
EH Bildu could win its first region-wide victory in the Basque Country, a shift that would set up conflict with a PP-Vox government.
Catalonia's ERC will be crucial to Sánchez's slim chances of forming a coalition.
Aragón has voted for the nationwide winner in every election since 1977, and polls suggest it will back the PP.

stories.headline: How Fashion Is Getting Heat Stress Wrong
stories.claim: Researchers at COP31 argue fashion's heat-stress risk is underestimated, with about 3% of garment workers at clinical heat stress at any time.
stories.summary: Researchers presenting at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya argue that the fashion industry is measuring heat risk for garment workers in the wrong way. Laurie Parsons of Royal Holloway says that room thermometers miss what happens inside workers' bodies, and that core temperature data show about 3% of the 70 million garment workers are in clinical heat stress at any given time. Over a year, 67% experience heat stress at least once, and pressing and washing roles face far higher exposure. Workers in Bangladesh, Cambodia and India face record heatwaves, and a Dhaka study found workers lose about 4.5% of annual income from heat-related absence. The findings point to a labour and health problem rather than only a space-cooling one.
key_points: Laurie Parsons told a Fair Labor Association panel at the COP31 Health Pavilion that heat is fundamentally a labour problem.

stories.headline: Hegseth Cements New Military Deal in Visit to Venezuela
stories.claim: US and Venezuela sign deal to restore military ties, including joint training and intelligence sharing, announced during Hegseth's Caracas visit.

The deal covers joint training and intelligence sharing, and Hegseth described Venezuela as having moved from a leading regional threat to a compliant security partner. The visit follows US forces capturing Nicolás Maduro in January and comes alongside an energy arrangement, brokered earlier this year, under which the US gains a role in tapping Venezuela's oil reserves. Hegseth linked the oil deal to the wider Iran war, saying it made the Strait of Hormuz 'a non-factor' for the Western Hemisphere. Few specifics were given on the military terms, and Washington is clearly seeking to deepen its influence in the country.

Negotiators are still wrangling over Made in Europe language, with the UK offering a weaker commitment than the EU's demand for alignment on trade defence measures. Burnham is expected to set out a 10-year plan in December, while the government considers a year-long national conversation in 2027.

stories.headline: World Court to rule whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
stories.claim: The ICJ is due to deliver its final judgment on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya on Thursday.
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice is set to rule on Thursday on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during the 2017 military crackdown in Rakhine state. That crackdown drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. No state has ever been found by the court to have committed genocide, so the ruling would be a landmark on state responsibility. The case was brought by The Gambia in 2019 with backing from the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Observers say it could also influence South Africa's genocide case against Israel. Myanmar has rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated and has argued it was conducting a counter-terrorism operation.
key_points: The ICJ will deliver its final judgment on Thursday 19 November in The Hague.
The Gambia filed the case in November 2019, backed by the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

stories.headline: Germany presses to make Ukraine aid Le Pen-proof
stories.claim: Germany is pushing to lock a durable EU funding scheme for Ukraine into the long-term budget, so it is hard to veto if Le Pen wins.
stories.summary: Germany is pushing to place a durable funding mechanism for Ukraine into the EU's next seven-year budget, designed to be hard for future opponents such as Marine Le Pen to block should she win France's presidential election in April. The plan would give the EU fiscal headroom to borrow beyond the €100 billion the Commission has proposed, with future decisions taken by qualified majority rather than unanimity. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made German support for the budget conditional on an extra €45 billion for Ukraine in 2027 and a financing perspective from 2028. Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia are expected to resist, and the issue will be negotiated before a special EU summit on 26–27 November. Merz's weak domestic position and the AfD's polling lead add pressure.
key_points: Berlin wants EU headroom to raise money for Ukraine beyond the €100 billion already proposed.
Future Ukraine funding decisions would need only qualified majority if Germany's plan prevails.

stories.headline: How Burnham tapped the brakes on his big Brexit reset
stories.claim: PM Andy Burnham is slowing his plans for a public Brexit debate, now pointing to mid-December for any EU options.
stories.summary: Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, promised two months ago a national conversation on Britain's long-term relationship with the EU, but he is now signalling a slower pace. Ahead of a long-awaited EU-UK summit on Friday, he hopes to secure deals on food standards, carbon emissions trading and youth mobility, plus assurances over the EU's Made in Europe scheme. Officials now suggest any options on the EU relationship could come in mid-December, possibly alongside his domestic 10-year plan due on 17 December, if viable options exist. Burnham says he has not ruled out rejoining the EU, but says there is 'no rush'. Politico spoke to more than 30 politicians and officials, and several questioned whether he has a clear strategy at all. The shift matters because it signals caution within Burnham's own Cabinet on Europe, a sensitive issue for markets and business.

stories.headline: Inside Ukraine’s Coalition of the Wobbling
stories.claim: Ukraine's Coalition of the Willing meets in Berlin, its first leaders' gathering since August, amid worries over weak leadership.
stories.summary: Ukraine's backers gather in Berlin on Thursday for the first leaders' meeting of the Coalition of the Willing since August, and the grouping looks weaker than it has in years. Its co-chairs, France, Germany and the UK, are all led by politically weakened leaders: Chancellor Friedrich Merz scraped through after a far-right surge, Emmanuel Macron is deeply unpopular, and Andy Burnham, the new UK prime minister, is still finding his feet on the world stage. Diplomats worry the group could be sidelined by any deal Donald Trump strikes with Vladimir Putin. The agenda covers legally binding security guarantees, a multinational force to guard a ceasefire, extra funding for next year and air defence. On Wednesday the European Commission proposed a €45 billion loan for Ukraine in 2027, and von der Leyen is seeking more money from non-EU countries.

stories.headline: Deutsche Bank leak: How 15m files put the bank on the spot
stories.claim: German regulator probes Deutsche Bank after 15 million leaked internal records surfaced, shares fell sharply.
stories.summary: Deutsche Bank faces a German data protection investigation after a leak of 15 million internal records, which shows the bank's shares sliding from recent highs. Hesse's data protection commissioner, Alexander Rossnagel, is checking whether the bank had adequate safeguards and whether it told affected people promptly. The files, published on November 17 under the banner "Inside Deutsche Bank" by a project led by a South African nonprofit, cover more than nine million emails and reach back to the early 2010s. Reported items include Epstein-linked payments, a 2017 mishandling of tax statements for 1,586 accounts including one belonging to Donald Trump, and a pre-invasion expansion plan for Russia. Frankfurt shares fell as much as 6.4% to €30.82 on Wednesday, and the New York listing closed down 5.47%. Deutsche Bank says the matters are old, that it expects no significant financial impact, and that the material is unverified by Reuters.

stories.headline: Investigators say Bayesian superyacht crew could not have known of wind risk
stories.claim: UK investigators say the superyacht Bayesian capsized in hurricane-force winds no crew could have anticipated, contrasting with Italian prosecutors' claims of crew error.
stories.summary: A UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch final report published on Thursday concludes that the superyacht Bayesian sank off Porticello, Sicily, because a downburst of hurricane-force winds, most likely from a thunderstorm, knocked it onto its side in under 15 seconds. The 56-metre yacht sank 18 minutes later on 19 August 2024, killing seven people, including tech entrepreneur Mike Lynch and his 18-year-old daughter Hannah. Investigators found the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down and its centreboard raised, so its vulnerability went unrecognised. The forecast had predicted gusts of only about 27 knots, while winds reached roughly 70 knots, and none of the life rafts inflated automatically. The MAIB makes seven recommendations to four agencies, including new rules for single-hulled sailing vessels and better severe-weather information for mariners. The findings diverge from Italian prosecutors, who have reportedly blamed crew error and are pursuing manslaughter charges against three crew members, and the MAIB warns its conclusions could change if withheld Italian evidence is disclosed.
key_points: The MAIB final report says the Bayesian was capsized by a downburst of hurricane-force winds in under 15 seconds.
The yacht had never been assessed at anchor with sails down and centreboard raised.

stories.headline: Foldable phones are finally getting the app support they deserve
stories.claim: Google Play will require foldable-ready apps to meet Tier 3 adaptive quality guidelines from April 2027.
stories.summary: Google is introducing foldable quality requirements for the Play Store, meaning developers must bring their apps up to Tier 3 of its Adaptive app quality guidelines from April 2027. Apps that fail to meet the threshold could be blocked from publishing or updating on Google Play, and may have reduced visibility. Developers will also need three foldable screenshots alongside the usual two phone screenshots, and games have until August 2027 for the full requirement. Existing apps will remain downloadable after the deadline. The move aims to make foldable phones work more smoothly, and it puts pressure on developers to adapt within about five months.

stories.headline: Elton John backs Australian artists in fight against AI in surprise Aria awards appearance
stories.claim: Elton John backs Australian artists' 'Not AI's To Take' campaign against AI copyright lobbying at the Aria awards.
stories.summary: Elton John used a pre-recorded message at the Aria awards in Sydney to back a campaign urging the Albanese government to stop AI companies using Australian creative work without permission and payment. The Not AI's To Take campaign is backed by dozens of groups across music, film, television, publishing and news, including News Corp, Foxtel, Seven Media and Guardian Australia. It warns that changes sought by AI firms could put Australia's $70bn creative industry and its 600,000 workers at risk. AI companies have argued that individual licensing is too difficult under current copyright law and have proposed an opt-out model, with Anthropic among them. The government, which says artists must be compensated, is expected to unveil a broader AI legislative package in late 2026 or early 2027.

This release is the first to add sound, from background noise to character dialogue, and adds an agent that builds worlds from conversation plus a gallery for sharing and remixing. Google DeepMind first showed the model to testers in October. The older Genie 3 now supports runs of up to three minutes, up from 60 seconds. The launch sits in a fast-growing field, after AMD agreed in September to buy Fei-Fei Li's World Labs for $8.2bn.

stories.headline: British hacker who stole $11m through text message scheme jailed for six years in US
stories.claim: British hacker Tyler Buchanan, linked to Scattered Spider, sentenced to six years in US prison for SMS phishing thefts.
stories.summary: A 24-year-old British hacker from Dundee has been sentenced to six years in a US federal prison for helping run a text-message phishing campaign that hit at least a dozen technology and telecoms firms and stole more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individuals. Tyler Buchanan began hacking as a teenager and was part of Scattered Spider, a loose collective of young English-speaking hackers blamed for a string of high-profile cyber-crimes. Prosecutors said the group made about $8m in under two years and used stolen credentials and SIM-swapping to target crypto investors in the US. The case closes a multi-country investigation involving the UK, US, Spain and Canada, and comes after Buchanan was arrested at Palma de Mallorca airport in May 2024. Officials say the case shows the growing threat from youth-led online crime groups.
key_points: Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, received a six-year federal prison sentence in the US for conspiracy to hack companies and steal cryptocurrency.
The group sent hundreds of fake work-login text messages, harvesting credentials through a Telegram bot and exposing confidential corporate data.
Prosecutors say the thefts exceeded $11.6m, with the largest single loss being $1.67m in December 2022.
Buchanan was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and extradited to the US; four American co-defendants have also pleaded guilty.
Two other Scattered Spider members were jailed in the UK in July, including for an attack that caused £39m of damage to Transport for London.

stories.headline: How Nvidia Chips Ended Up Within Reach of China’s Military
stories.claim: Court records show alleged smuggling of Nvidia GPUs to China via fake front companies, despite US export bans.
stories.summary: Court records describe a smuggling scheme in which three men allegedly moved Nvidia AI chips to buyers in China despite a US ban. In a March 2024 WeChat exchange, one alleged participant pitched the chips as lucrative, and a partner allegedly told him to remove all references to China to avoid attracting US government attention. Data centre electricity use is forecast to double to 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030 under current policies. The IEA also says the world now uses more energy for cooling than heating for the first time.

stories.summary: US studio CLB Architects has completed Wiley, a compact accessory dwelling unit on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, just outside the ski town of Jackson. The 1,000 square foot limit set by local rules shaped a two-storey, gabled building clad in dark corrugated metal and cedar. The clients, an empty-nester couple, built much of it themselves over about nine months, and the design includes a climbing wall used by their son. The project is presented as a model for accommodating growth in the Mountain West while preserving open land. It is an architectural case study with limited wider market impact.

The house is limited to 1,000 square feet under local regulations and sits on a one-acre riverside plot.

stories.headline: How a Former New York City Caviar Factory Became an Art-Filled Oasis of Calm
stories.claim: Spanish-born producer Alexis Piqueras's Tribeca loft, once a 19th-century caviar factory, has been stripped back into a calm, art-filled home.
stories.summary: A former 19th-century caviar factory in Tribeca, Manhattan, has been turned into a calm, art-filled loft by Spanish-born producer and AP Studio founder Alexis Piqueras. Working with Brazilian-born designer Pali Xisto Cornelsen, he pared back earlier renovations, keeping original brick walls, timber columns and wood windows with views of the Hudson River across roughly 2,500 square feet. The kitchen got white-painted fronts and solid-cherry pulls, the walls were finished in Benjamin Moore's Simply White, and recessed lighting was removed. The collection leans towards queer artists, including Wolfgang Tillmans, Peter Hujar, David Wojnarowicz and David Hockney, alongside vintage Scandinavian and modernist furniture by Charlotte Perriand, Alvar Aalto and Isamu Noguchi. It is a lifestyle feature rather than news, with no market relevance.
key_points: Piqueras moved back to New York from a three-year stint in Los Angeles and wanted a quiet retreat from city life.
The loft occupies a former 19th-century caviar factory in Tribeca and keeps its original brick, timber and wood windows.
Designer Pali Xisto Cornelsen stripped out earlier updates, painted the walls Simply White and removed recessed lighting.

stories.headline: Nike CFO Says It Will Take Two Years for Jordan Brand to Return to Growth
stories.claim: Nike's CFO says Jordan Brand revenue will dip slightly until 2031 and the four key franchises will shrink by $7bn from peak.
stories.summary: Nike's new chief financial officer, Dave Denton, used the company's first investor day in nine years to lay out a slow recovery. Jordan Brand revenue is expected to fall slightly over fiscal 2027 to 2031, with modest growth only from fiscal 2029. Denton said that Air Force 1, Air Jordan 1, Dunk and Chuck Taylor, which generated about $13 billion at their peak in fiscal 2024, are expected to fall to around $6 billion by the end of fiscal 2027. The news confirms how deep the reset at the sportswear giant runs.

stories.headline: Ukraine strikes and partly collapses Crimean Bridge
stories.claim: Ukraine says it severely damaged the Crimean Bridge, with a large arch of the road span collapsing into the Kerch Strait and road traffic halted.
stories.summary: Ukraine has severely damaged the Crimean Bridge, with a large arched section of the road span apparently collapsing into the Kerch Strait and cutting the peninsula's direct road link to Russia. Zelensky called it an "unprecedented operation" prepared over weeks, describing a seven-stage attack that suppressed air defences before Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles and drones struck the span. Ukraine's military says the roadway is out of action and no vehicles can cross, while the rail section is standing with a damaged arch; rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday. A second wave of drones reportedly relayed radio signals after Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starshield was restricted, which Zelensky said hampered drone control, though SpaceX denies any slowdown. The Kremlin said Putin was briefed, the bridge would be restored "even better than before", and Russia's Investigative Committee opened a terrorism case. The bridge cost $3.6bn to build and was opened by Putin in 2018. The strike comes just before a planned meeting in Shenzhen between Putin, Trump and Xi Jinping on the sidelines of Apec, and it disrupts a key supply route for Russia's southern army. Russia's defence ministry reported 2,256 Ukrainian drones downed in a second day of record attacks.

stories.headline: Rubio says zero evidence US tech outages were caused by hostile actor, after Mullin AI theory
stories.claim: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is 'zero evidence' that recent US tech outages were caused by a hostile actor, rejecting an AI-related theory floated by Mullin.
stories.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is "zero evidence" that a series of recent nationwide tech outages was linked to or caused by a malicious or hostile actor, and that the country is not under systemic attack. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin backed that view, saying the homeland is secure and no cyberattack caused the disruptions, which affected millions and included an FAA ground stop. Mullin had earlier told Fox News that an unnamed expert suggested advanced AI systems could be overwhelming older infrastructure, a theory he called plausible but unproven and said he was 98% sure was not a cyberattack. Reproductive rights groups welcomed the decision, and Overton had called for strict regulation of the abortion pill mifepristone. The FDA is left without a nominee, and the White House must now choose a replacement.

stories.headline: Nvidia posts record results under interim CEO Kress as board rules out Huang's return
stories.claim: Nvidia beat expectations with record third-quarter results as its board ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang and named Colette Kress interim CEO.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board has ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, chair Harvey Jones said on the company's third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday, even as the chipmaker beat Wall Street forecasts. Huang resigned on 12 November after disclosing extramarital relationships, including one with a woman US officials suspect of links to Chinese intelligence, a claim that remains unproven and that China denies. The board has hired Heidrick & Struggles to run a thorough search covering internal and external candidates, with CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO. A national security and export controls committee has been created, and an independent investigation and an SEC probe are under way. Reports say the board approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas, and Huang, who had said he would be honoured to return, has been rebuffed. The decision disappoints investors and staff who had backed his return, including Elon Musk and Donald Trump.

stories.headline: UK climate advisers warn weakening EV mandate would make missing carbon budgets likely
stories.claim: UK climate advisers warn that weakening the EV mandate would likely leave Britain missing its legally binding climate targets.
stories.summary: The UK's Climate Change Committee has warned ministers that weakening the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate would likely leave Britain off track for its legally binding climate targets. In a letter published on Wednesday to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, chair Nigel Topping estimated that loosening the rules could add up to 15 million barrels of extra oil use a year by 2030, costing motorists more than £1 billion at current prices, and about 8.4 million tonnes of CO2 a year by the next decade. He argued that keeping current rules could save a typical household around £800 a year. The warning follows a Guardian report that ministers plan to cut the 2030 EV sales target from 80% by about a quarter to around 60%, after a consultation that closed last month. Electric cars made up 26.6% of new UK car sales in the first ten months of 2026, against a 33% headline target, and carmakers have lobbied for cuts as low as 50% or 60%. The government says it has not yet decided and remains committed to the 2030 petrol and diesel phase-out and to 100% zero-emission sales by 2035. The debate matters because a weaker mandate could force the government to amend carbon budgets or find other emissions cuts.
key_points: The Climate Change Committee published a letter from chair Nigel Topping to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday warning against weakening the ZEV mandate.
Loosening the rules could add up to 15 million barrels of oil use a year by 2030, costing over £1 billion at current prices.
The CCC estimates weaker rules could add 8.4 million tonnes of CO2 a year by the next decade and say the UK would likely miss its legal climate targets.
The Guardian reported ministers plan to cut the 2030 EV sales target from 80% to about 60%, after a consultation that closed last month.
Electric cars were 26.6% of new UK car sales in the first ten months of 2026, against a 33% headline target.
The government says it has not decided on the interim target and remains committed to the 2030 petrol and diesel phase-out and 100% zero-emission sales by 2035.
stories.market_take: Looser EV rules would ease pressure on carmakers, though the outcome remains a consultation with no final decision.

stories.headline: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
stories.claim: Anthropic's IPO is set to list on Nasdaq on Thursday, with 825m shares priced at $70 to $78 each.
stories.summary: Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is heading for one of the largest stock market flotations in history, with shares due to list on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday. The prospectus offers 825 million class A shares at an indicative price of $70 to $78, with the final price to be set on Wednesday. Voting power is structured so that the shares represent only 49.9% of total votes, limiting buyers' ability to influence the company. The Guardian explainer says retail investors can buy at listing through brokers, and that funds such as Baillie Gifford's trusts and Fidelity products already hold stakes. Commentators flag governance concerns, a lack of consistent profitability and the volatility seen after SpaceX's June listing.
key_points: 825 million class A shares are on offer, with an indicative IPO price of $70 to $78 each.
The final price will be set on Wednesday, with trading on Nasdaq expected on Thursday.
Class A shares carry votes that total only 49.9% of the overall voting power.
Retail investors will be able to buy alongside institutions at the offering.
The prospectus includes 92 pages on risks, and analysts point to capital intensity and no consistent profit record.
Commentators note SpaceX's shares have at times traded below their IPO price since its June listing.
stories.market_take: A very large listing could draw heavy capital and influence tech sentiment, with early volatility likely after the debut.

stories.headline: Nvidia’s startup stakes ballooned to $65B, but Huang’s exit puts future deals in doubt
stories.claim: Nvidia's private equity stakes rose to $65.5bn, but VCs expect less startup funding now that Huang is leaving.
stories.summary: Nvidia disclosed on Tuesday that its stakes in private companies are now worth $65.5 billion, up from $22 billion in January, after it invested $16 billion in equities in the latest quarter and $58 billion over nine months. The chipmaker has backed nearly 350 startups, including Anthropic and OpenAI, and has $118 billion in guarantees, mostly a backstop for OpenAI's Ohio data centre. Interim CFO Kress said Nvidia will keep financing strong customers but will rigorously assess future commitments, and that it intends to return excess free cash flow to shareholders. Investors expect a more cautious approach after Jensen Huang's exit, with fewer and smaller startup cheques. The story signals a possible pullback in venture capital from one of its largest backers.
key_points: Nvidia's equity stakes in private and public companies are valued at $65.5bn, up from $22bn in January.
The company invested $16bn in equities in the latest quarter and $58bn over the first nine months of its fiscal year.
Nvidia has backed nearly 350 startups, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Thinking Machines and Lambda, according to PitchBook.
It has $118bn in guarantees, with $105bn tied to the backstop for OpenAI's $500bn Ohio data centre.
Interim leader Kress said Nvidia will return excess free cash flow to shareholders and review future commitments more strictly.

stories.headline: Waymo pauses driverless taxis on all US freeways after California ban
stories.claim: California's DMV has barred Waymo driverless vehicles from state freeways, and Waymo has paused freeway rides across all US markets.
stories.summary: Waymo has temporarily pulled its driverless taxis off all US freeways after California's Department of Motor Vehicles banned them from state motorways, effective 11 November. The regulator called the vehicles an "imminent hazard to public safety" after repeated incursions into active construction zones, including a 5 November incident in which several driverless cars entered a closure on US Route 101 south of San Francisco. A separate 6 November episode showed a Waymo apparently trying to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles slowing traffic on a San Francisco highway, and the DMV also cited a similar earlier incident on 18 May. Waymo says no one was injured and there were no collisions, and it has suspended freeway service in other markets including Phoenix, Austin and Miami, while continuing to test with safety drivers. The restriction stays in place until Waymo shows the regulator it has fixed the problems. City-street service continues as normal. The move is a setback for the Alphabet-owned company, which runs driverless taxis in 15 US cities and completes around half a million trips a week.

stories.headline: CISA warns of critical Java flaw as US tech outages prompt questions
stories.claim: CISA urges immediate patching of a critical Java flaw dubbed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), which Oracle fixed in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update.
stories.summary: US cyber agency CISA issued an alert on Tuesday urging organisations to patch a critical vulnerability in Oracle's Java platform, dubbed Java4Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-114938. The memory-corruption flaw sits in the Base64 decoder of the HotSpot JVM within the Java Development Kit and could let unauthenticated attackers crash systems or run code remotely. Oracle fixed the issue in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update across several Java SE versions, though it has not publicly acknowledged the bug, and rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1 while researchers rate it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. The start-up Calif says it used artificial intelligence to find the flaw. Java is used by about 90% of Fortune 500 companies and underpins many banks, hospitals and government agencies, so exposure is broad, and enterprise software such as Jenkins, Jira, Confluence and Keycloak may be affected. CISA advises reviewing software inventories, since Java may be hidden in third-party apps and containers. It is unclear whether any platforms have been hit. The disclosure comes amid a string of outages, though the NSA said its outage was routine maintenance rather than confirmed as linked. Insurers may treat it as the start of patching deadlines.
key_points: CISA issued an alert on Tuesday urging immediate patching of CVE-2026-114938, dubbed Java4Shell.
The flaw in the Base64 decoder of the HotSpot JVM can let unauthenticated attackers crash systems or run code remotely.
Oracle fixed the bug in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update but has not publicly acknowledged it.
Oracle rates the flaw 8.1 under CVSS 3.1; researchers rate it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0.
Cyber start-up Calif says it used AI to find the flaw, weeks after a PHP flaw affecting around 30 million websites.
Java is used by about 90% of Fortune 500 companies; CISA advises checking for hidden Java in third-party apps and containers.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect, though cyber insurers and security vendors may see renewed attention.

stories.headline: Amazon MGM names Robert Pattinson as next James Bond, directed by Villeneuve
stories.claim: Robert Pattinson has been named the seventh James Bond, with Denis Villeneuve directing the 26th film for Amazon MGM.
stories.summary: Robert Pattinson has been unveiled as the next James Bond, the seventh actor to play 007, succeeding Daniel Craig. Jeff Bezos, speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley event in California, said he was "heavily involved" in the casting and had initially been biased against casting such a famous actor, but screen tests made the choice "so obvious." The 26th Bond film, due in 2028, will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and is the first made since Amazon MGM took over the franchise after buying MGM in 2022, making it the first Bond film without Broccoli family creative control since 1962. The title and exact release date have not been announced. Insiders see Pattinson as a bankable pick at a time when cinemas are struggling to attract audiences. The film follows No Time to Die in 2021, which ended with Bond's death.

stories.headline: US extends AI chip export curbs to more countries and closes China remote-access loophole
stories.claim: The US Commerce Department imposed licence requirements on advanced AI chip exports to five Southeast Asian and Latin American countries and closed a remote-access loophole for Chinese firms.
stories.summary: The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule on Monday, 16 November, requiring licences to export advanced chips and servers to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, which Washington considers higher-risk for diversion to China. The rule closes a loophole that let Chinese firms rent computing power through overseas data centres, shifting compliance duties to cloud operators, who must meet new 'Know Your Customer's Workload' checks. Subsidiaries of US companies and data centres running only commercial recommendation systems are exempt, and applications will be reviewed case by case. Nvidia shares fell as much as 2.9% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped up to 5.5% on the news. Analyst Neil Shah of Counterpoint called it a severe short-term bottleneck for Chinese tech giants and a long-term catalyst for decoupling toward domestic chips such as Huawei's Ascend. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly wants Megaspeed's chip access cut, and he and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick disagree on how hard to press. The rule landed as Trump travelled to Asia to meet Xi Jinping.
key_points: BIS issued an interim final rule on 16 November requiring licences for advanced AI chip exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.
The rule closes a loophole that let Chinese firms remotely use US chips through overseas data centres.
Cloud operators must meet new 'Know Your Customer's Workload' checks.
Nvidia fell as much as 2.9% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped up to 5.5%.
Bessent reportedly wants Megaspeed's chip access cut, and officials are divided on how hard to press China.
Subsidiaries of US companies and commercial recommender-system data centres are exempt.

stories.headline: Congress moves to tighten AI chip export rules to China after Nvidia spy scandal
stories.claim: Bipartisan momentum in Washington is building for tighter AI chip export controls on China, with a possible law by year-end.
stories.summary: Bipartisan momentum is building in Washington for tighter controls on advanced AI chip exports to China, with a possible law by the end of the year. House Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries both favour stronger controls, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune sees a 'high probability' of more restrictions. Three bills, the Chip Security Act, the MATCH Act and the AI Overwatch Act, sit in the Senate's version of the defence authorisation bill, though no final text has been agreed; Senator John Kennedy puts the odds of passage better than even. The push follows the Huang affair and reports that Nvidia sold $4 billion of chips to Singapore firm Megaspeed, which is suspected of diverting them to China and is under Justice Department investigation. Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott has asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, and the Remote Access Security Act is being revived. Schumer has said Huang and the Trump administration must answer to Congress.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune sees a 'high probability' Congress will impose more restrictions.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin set for first trilateral nuclear talks at APEC in Shenzhen
stories.claim: Trump, Xi and Putin are set to hold the first trilateral meeting on nuclear arms control on the sidelines of APEC in Shenzhen, with no agreement expected.
stories.summary: The White House has confirmed that Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin will meet on Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, which would be the first in-person meeting of the three leaders, though China has not formally confirmed it. Nuclear arms reduction is expected to be the main topic, with Iran possibly raised and Ukraine reportedly not on the agenda, but a senior US official said no agreement is expected. The meeting follows the expiry of the New START treaty in February, which left no major arms control limits between Washington and Moscow. Trump wants a new treaty that includes China, which has rejected joining trilateral nuclear talks, saying it is neither fair nor realistic at this stage. Trump arrived late on Wednesday for the two-day summit and holds a bilateral lunch with Xi before the trilateral, their fourth meeting since 2025. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the agenda and format had not yet been agreed. China's Foreign Ministry called the meeting of groundbreaking significance, and UN chief Antonio Guterres said the UN would support any denuclearisation effort. Trump is also on a four-day Asia trip including a Quad meeting and a US-ASEAN summit in Manila, and the Yalta comparison has drawn commentary.
key_points: The White House confirmed a Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting on Thursday in Shenzhen, though China has not formally confirmed it.

stories.headline: PM Burnham says Brexit has not worked as UK prepares to sign EU food reset deal
stories.claim: PM Andy Burnham says Brexit 'has not worked' and will sign a UK-EU reset deal at a Friday summit in Brussels, drawing Conservative and Reform opposition.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who succeeded Keir Starmer, said Brexit "has not worked" and that Britain has lost more than it gained, as he prepares to sign a new agreement with the EU at a summit on Friday. The package covers food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme allowing about 80,000 EU nationals under 30 to live and work in Britain for three years. It is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP, about £17bn, with food-specific gains of about £5bn, according to relations minister Hamish Falconer, who said the UK would get a "voice in the room" but no vote on EU food rules. An exit clause is under consideration so a future government could not easily reverse closer alignment; a draft text reportedly would make a leaving party pay for restoring border controls, which EU diplomats call the "Farage clause" while UK sources call it routine. The Conservatives and Reform have pledged to undo the reset if elected. Boris Johnson said Britain would "absolutely" vote for Brexit again, and Nigel Farage called the stance a "total betrayal". The National Farmers' Union welcomed fewer checks but wants carve-outs and transitional arrangements. Options on the longer-term relationship, including rejoining the single market or customs union, will inform the next parliament.
key_points: Burnham said Brexit "has not worked" in a speech at the Lord Mayor's Banquet, arguing Britain has lost more than it gained.
The reset deal is due to be signed at a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO over affair with suspected Chinese spy; Kress interim CEO
stories.claim: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on 12 November over disclosed affairs; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and the board is searching for a successor.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board has ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, with chair Harvey Jones saying so on the company's third-quarter earnings call, even as the chipmaker beat Wall Street forecasts. Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member on 12 November after admitting extramarital affairs, one reportedly with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive whom US officials suspect was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security; Beijing calls the claims a smear. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim chief executive, and Harvey Jones became the company's first independent chair. Shares fell as much as 14% in early trading after the resignation and closed down just over 4%, with roughly $1 trillion of market value lost that month. The Financial Times reported Huang was discussing a return and a petition gathered more than 115,000 signatures, but the board has now rebuffed him. Nvidia may lack full insurance cover for executive conduct, raising lawsuit risk.
key_points: Nvidia's board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that Huang will not be reinstated as CEO.

stories.claim: The US has lost its measles elimination status, prompting Democratic attacks on RFK Jr. and the Trump administration.
stories.summary: The United States has lost its measles elimination status for the first time in more than 25 years, according to the Pan American Health Organization, which also downgraded Mexico and Bolivia. The US has recorded more than 7,700 cases over two years, with over 10 deaths reported. Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, have blamed Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the Trump administration. Kennedy said he recommends the MMR vaccine and blamed pandemic-era disruptions for gaps in childhood immunisation. The CDC said the designation does not itself protect people, and that vaccination does.
key_points: The PAHO announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status.
The US has recorded more than 7,700 cases of measles in two years, with deaths reported in multiple states.
Mexico and Bolivia were also stripped of the status.
Democrats, including Schumer, blame RFK Jr. and the administration for the resurgence.
Kennedy says COVID-era disruptions caused vaccination gaps and recommends the MMR vaccine.

stories.headline: EQT Ventures Invests $10 Million in Enterprise AI Company Edra
stories.claim: EQT Ventures has invested about $10 million in enterprise AI start-up Edra after using its software internally.
stories.summary: EQT Ventures, the investment arm of Swedish group EQT, has put about $10 million into Edra, an enterprise AI software company, lifting its total funding to around $40 million. The cheque followed a four-week trial in which EQT used Edra's platform in its IT services division, and the group has kept using it and plans to roll it out more widely. The new money extends a Series A of roughly $30 million earlier in 2026, led by Sequoia Capital with participation from 8VC and A*. Edra, founded in 2024 by two former Palantir engineers, offices in New York and London, builds software that documents how companies carry out procedures and turns that knowledge into instructions for AI agents. EQT is also offering Edra access to its portfolio of more than 330 companies.
key_points: EQT Ventures invested about $10 million in Edra, taking its total funding to roughly $40 million.

Edra's product documents company procedures and converts them into instructions AI agents can execute, rather than a simple question-answering assistant.
EQT plans to extend the platform across its more than 330 portfolio companies in the Americas, Europe and Asia.

stories.headline: Baidu’s Robin Li Says AI Needs Monetization to Avoid Bubble Risk
stories.claim: Baidu chief Robin Li warns AI bubble fears could become reality unless heavy spending produces profits.
stories.summary: Robin Li, chairman and chief executive of Baidu, has warned that concerns about an AI bubble could become reality if heavy investment fails to produce higher profits. Speaking at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday, he said AI spending had yet to generate significant revenue or profit for most companies. He split the industry into four layers (chips, cloud infrastructure, large models and applications) and argued that competition is fiercest at the foundation level, while value will ultimately be captured at the application layer. He also said Baidu has launched a Token Exchange connecting AI token providers with enterprise and individual customers to ease computing shortages. Li remained optimistic that AI is an inevitable trend.
key_points: Li said spending on AI had yet to produce significant revenue or profit gains for most companies.
He warned the AI bubble concern could become reality if monetisation does not follow.
He divided AI into chips, cloud infrastructure, large models and applications, saying value will ultimately sit at the application layer.
Baidu has launched a 'Token Exchange' linking AI token providers with enterprise and individual buyers to ease compute shortages.
Li said he remained optimistic that AI is an inevitable trend.
The remarks were made at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on 17 November.
stories.market_take: Comments like these may weigh modestly on AI-exposed tech stocks if investors doubt returns on spending.

stories.headline: South Africa’s Rand Tests 17 Per Dollar as Political Risks Rise
stories.claim: South African rand briefly touched 17 per dollar, its weakest since April, amid a stronger dollar and local political tensions.
stories.summary: The South African rand briefly touched 17 to the US dollar on Tuesday 17 November, its weakest level since April, before easing to about 16.92. The rand closed at 16.42 on 4 November and at 16.98 on 16 November, a 3.4% fall for the dollar over that stretch. Analysts at TreasuryONE blamed dollar strength, a hawkish US Federal Reserve, local politics and weaker emerging-market sentiment. Over the same period the euro fell 2.1% and the Brazilian real lost 5.9% against the dollar. After the local elections, the Electoral Commission declared results on 8 November, with the ANC on about 31% and the DA on about 24.6% nationally, and many municipalities remain hung. The ANC and DA both sit in the national unity government, so local coalition deals could strain it.
key_points: The rand briefly hit 17 per dollar in Asian trade on 17 November, before easing to about 16.92.
The currency closed at 16.42 on 4 November (election day) and 16.98 on 16 November, a 3.4% move against it.
TreasuryONE analyst Wichard Cilliers cited dollar strength, a hawkish Federal Reserve, local politics and weaker EM sentiment.
The euro fell 2.1% and the Brazilian real 5.9% against the dollar over 4 to 16 November, so the move is broader than South Africa alone.
Local elections produced many hung municipalities, with Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni lacking published coalition deals as of 17 November.
A weaker rand raises import costs such as fuel and reduces the dollar value of South African assets for foreign investors.
stories.market_take: Political risk pressure could push the rand weaker and weigh on South African assets.

stories.headline: Germany's Uniper expects core profit of up to €1.5 billion in 2027
stories.claim: Uniper guides 2027 core profit of €1.2–1.5bn and sets out €6bn investment plan ahead of a possible re-listing.
stories.summary: Germany's state-backed utility Uniper expects 2027 core profit of €1.2 billion to €1.5 billion, up from €1.1 billion to €1.3 billion forecast for 2026. It also detailed €6 billion ($6.6 billion) of investments through the early 2030s, with around two-thirds going to gas-fired plants and conversions for data centres, and 25% to 30% to renewables. Uniper has about 700 megawatts of grid capacity for data-centre projects in Germany, Britain, the Netherlands or Sweden, and CEO Michael Lewis said three projects are at an advanced stage. Berlin, which spent €13.5 billion rescuing the company in 2022, is cutting its 99.12% stake to a blocking minority, either through a sale or a re-listing, with the listing preferred. Sources have put a possible sale valuation at under €10 billion to over €14 billion.
key_points: Uniper expects 2027 core profit of €1.2 billion to €1.5 billion, against €1.1 billion to €1.3 billion guided for 2026.

stories.headline: Oligarch’s ex-wife to claim £600mn for ‘reasonable needs’ in London divorce case
stories.claim: Natalia Potanina seeks £600mn in needs-based claim in London divorce from sanctioned tycoon Vladimir Potanin, with trial starting at the High Court.
stories.summary: The ex-wife of sanctioned Russian tycoon Vladimir Potanin is seeking £600 million for her 'reasonable needs' in what is described as Britain's biggest ever divorce trial. Natalia Potanina, 65, is also asking for a £150 million home and a £441 million maintenance fund if her main claim fails, and wants the Russian property known as The Autumn House. Her lawyers say she earned her share by caring for their three children over 30 years of marriage. Potanin's lawyers call the demands 'totally out of proportion' and say she has already received £63 million. The case, launched in 2018, is due to begin at the High Court, and it is set against a record UK settlement of £554 million from 2021.
